source.title: Interpretable Neuron Structuring with Graph Spectral Regularization
source.authors: Alexander Tong; D. van Dijk; Jay S. Stanley; Matthew Amodio; Kristina M. Yim; R. Muhle; James P. Noonan; Guy Wolf; Smita Krishnaswamy

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results about organizing hidden-layer features with graph spectral regularization, but does not test any of the listed claim versions or rely on the claim as a tool or assumption.
record.gate_note: The paper does not estimate the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs, test explanations on held-out activations, or evaluate attribution graphs. The qualitative feature-organization findings below are related to the topic but do not measure any listed version. MNIST accuracy and computation-time comparisons are not rows because they do not measure the claim's object.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes graph spectral regularization to organize hidden units in small dense networks and capsule nets (MNIST, synthetic and single-cell data). It shows qualitative, group-level structure. It reports no share of interpretable or single-job neurons, uses no language models or InceptionV1, has no attribution graphs, and does not score explanations on held-out activations. Its regularizer effect is near V4's theme, but V4 concerns the share of interpretable neurons in vision and language models, which is never measured here.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that GSR makes coherent, interpretable features emerge, and that learning the graph reveals structure relevant to the data. They add that GSR costs little performance (Table 1).
record.recipe_differences: The study trains networks with graph-Laplacian regularization to organize hidden-layer activations. It does not use the neuron-explanation or held-out activation-testing procedures described in the claim.

fits_no_version.finding: A graph Laplacian penalty on a hidden layer localizes activations by class (MNIST grid). It also orders capsule dimensions consistently, e.g. one dimension for line thickness. Learned graphs recover cluster, hierarchy and trajectory structure that a standard autoencoder or beta-VAE does not show.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularizing relationships among hidden units makes group-level feature structure easier to interpret in small dense networks.

record.peer_reviewed: International Symposium on Intelligent Data Analysis
record.problems: The interpretability outcomes relevant here are qualitative and do not quantify an interpretable share or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.rows_left_out: The MNIST classification accuracy and computation-time results in Section 4.3 and Table 1 were left out because they measure task performance and cost, not neuron interpretability or any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B and no neuron-pole job shares.
All: no language models, mixture-of-experts models or scale comparison.
All: no InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose or recursive generalization.
The interpretable-neuron share and its rise with tools or architecture. GSR improves group-level visual organization but gives no share, and no InceptionV1-sized estimates.
All: no attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.
All: explanations are not tested for predicting where neurons fire.
All: no simulation-based scoring of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Two results are not recorded as rows: the synthetic cluster-count result (Fig. 3) and the T-cell trajectory result (Fig. 4). Both bear on no version, so their omission does not matter here. The interpretability evidence is qualitative and concerns groups of units, not single-neuron jobs. The study's subjects (small MNIST classifiers, autoencoders, capsule nets) are far from the claim's subjects (large language models, InceptionV1).

versions.untested_parts: The share of poles with one or two jobs and the share not understood.
Interpretability shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, and recursive generalization.
The proposed causes of messy neurons, the effect of architecture and tools on interpretable share, and the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: MNIST classifier
rows.operation_detail: Applied graph spectral regularization to an 8x8 grid-structured layer; added three convolutional layers after the regularized layer.
rows.measure: Whether activation patterns form localized, class-associated receptive fields that can be interpreted from the input.
rows.baseline: Without GSR, activations are described as unstructured and difficult to interpret by class.
rows.value: With GSR, digit representations occupy specific areas; activation patterns are described as corresponding to digit type, including a misclassified 9 activating in the 7 region.
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Enforcing Grid Structure on Mnist; Fig. 1
rows.note: Qualitative account of localized activations and their semantic interpretation; it does not assess single-neuron pole explanations or report an interpretable-neuron share.

rows.subject: capsule net
rows.operation_detail: Applied GSR using 16 fully connected graphs between the 10 digit capsules.

conditions.value: 16 fully connected graphs between digit capsules

rows.measure: Consistency and interpretability of feature ordering across digit capsules.
rows.baseline: In the standard capsule network, feature ordering is described as random across capsules.
rows.value: With GSR, node 1 is described as corresponding to line thickness across all digits.
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Enforcing Node Consistency on Capsule Networks; Fig. 2
rows.note: This is a shared feature across capsule representations, not a test of the claim's neuron-pole job estimates.

rows.subject: graph spectral regularized model
rows.operation_detail: Applied graph spectral regularization to a six-node layer with three connected node pairs.

conditions.value: generated data with three large-scale structures, each comprising two Gaussian subclusters in 15 dimensions
six nodes in three connected pairs

rows.measure: Whether the learned node groups represent the large-scale clusters and their subclusters.
rows.baseline: The paper says the data structure is not clear with a standard autoencoder or β-VAE.
rows.value: Each node pair acts as a super node detecting one large-scale cluster; the two nodes encode its two Gaussian substructures.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Clusters within Clusters on Generated Data; Fig. 5
rows.note: A qualitative result about groups of units representing hierarchical data structure, not a measurement of individual neuron jobs.

rows.subject: graph spectral regularized autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Learned a feature graph with GSR in an autoencoder.

conditions.value: mouse cortex single-cell RNA-sequencing data: over 4000 cells and over 8000 genes

rows.measure: Whether learned components and their within-component activation structure correspond to cell types and developmental progression.
rows.baseline: With a standard autoencoder, the paper says the progression from intermediate progenitors to mature neurons is not visible.
rows.value: The learned graph has six components described as meta-features; the largest component shows progression from intermediate progenitors toward mature neurons.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Hierarchical Cluster and Trajectory Structure on Developing Mouse Cortex Data; Fig. 6
rows.note: The paper relates graph components and activation patterns to cell types and progression; it does not test held-out explanations of individual neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
